claim: The neural processing of faces and bodies is often studied separately, despite their natural integration in perception.
source: The neural processing of faces and bodies is often studied separately, despite their natural integration in perception.
evidence: This is a statement about the research field presented in the introduction without specific data or citations in this sentence.

claim: STS neurons showed selectivity for specific combinations of head–body orientations.
source: STS neurons showed selectivity for specific combinations of head–body orientations.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anterior STS (aSTS) neurons enabled more reliable decoding of head–body configuration angles compared to middle STS neurons.
source: Anterior STS (aSTS) neurons enabled more reliable decoding of head–body configuration angles compared to middle STS neurons.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by decoding analyses presented in the results.

claim: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was lowest for head–body angle pairs differing only in sign (e.g. head–body orientation difference of ±90° relative to the anatomical midline).
source: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was lowest for head–body angle pairs differing only in sign (e.g. head–body orientation difference of ±90° relative to the anatomical midline), and highest for aligned (0°) head–body orientations versus those with maximum angular difference.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by decoding analyses shown in figures.

claim: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was highest for aligned (0°) head–body orientations versus those with maximum angular difference.
source: Decoding accuracy in aSTS was lowest for head–body angle pairs differing only in sign (e.g. head–body orientation difference of ±90° relative to the anatomical midline), and highest for aligned (0°) head–body orientations versus those with maximum angular difference.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by decoding analyses shown in figures.

claim: Inverted bodies showed diminished decoding of head–body orientation angle compared to upright bodies.
source: Inverted bodies showed diminished decoding of head–body orientation angle compared to upright bodies.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experiment 3 data.

claim: aSTS integrates head and body orientation cues, revealing configuration-specific neural mechanisms.
source: These findings show that aSTS integrates head and body orientation cues, revealing configuration-specific neural mechanisms, and advance our understanding of social perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Behavioral and fMRI studies in humans suggest that face and body processing interact.
source: Despite the distinct research traditions, behavioral and fMRI studies in humans suggest that face and body processing interact (Hu et al., 2020; Taubert et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Face-selective units in macaque mid superior temporal sulcus (STS) face-selective patches respond to an object occluding a face on top of a body.
source: Furthermore, face-selective units in macaque mid superior temporal sulcus (STS) face-selective patches respond to an object occluding a face on top of a body (Arcaro et al., 2020), which agrees with monkey (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015) and human fMRI (Cox et al., 2004) studies that showed that a blurred head on top of a body can activate face-selective regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arcaro et al., 2020.

claim: A blurred head on top of a body can activate face-selective regions in monkeys and humans.
source: Furthermore, face-selective units in macaque mid superior temporal sulcus (STS) face-selective patches respond to an object occluding a face on top of a body (Arcaro et al., 2020), which agrees with monkey (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015) and human fMRI (Cox et al., 2004) studies that showed that a blurred head on top of a body can activate face-selective regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fisher and Freiwald, 2015 and Cox et al., 2004.

claim: Anterior inferior temporal (IT) neurons respond stronger to face–body configurations in which the face is located at its natural position on top of the body than to unnatural face–body configurations.
source: Recently, we showed that anterior inferior temporal (IT) neurons respond stronger to face–body configurations in which the face is located at its natural position on top of the body than to unnatural face–body configurations, showing that the face and body interact in a configuration-specific manner in IT (Zafirova et al., 2024; Zafirova et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The face and body interact in a configuration-specific manner in IT.
source: Recently, we showed that anterior inferior temporal (IT) neurons respond stronger to face–body configurations in which the face is located at its natural position on top of the body than to unnatural face–body configurations, showing that the face and body interact in a configuration-specific manner in IT (Zafirova et al., 2024; Zafirova et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The responses of most face-selective STS neurons are modulated by the 3D orientation of the head.
source: The responses of most face-selective STS neurons are modulated by the 3D orientation of the head (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Perrett et al., 1992; Perrett et al., 1984; Perrett et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The responses of most body-selective STS neurons are sensitive to body orientation.
source: Likewise, the responses of most body-selective STS neurons are sensitive to body orientation (Bao et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both head and body orientation are important social cues, for example for the attention of a viewed agent or the direction of an agent's action.
source: This might not be surprising because both head and body orientation are important social cues, for example for the attention of a viewed agent or the direction of an agent's action.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about social perception.

claim: Human psychophysical studies showed that body and head orientation interact in social perception.
source: Our study was also motivated by human psychophysical studies that showed that body and head orientation interact in social perception (Hietanen, 2002; Moors et al., 2015; Vrancken et al., 2017), although it is unclear at which level – sensory or higher – the observed interactions occurred.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is unclear at which level – sensory or higher – the observed interactions between body and head orientation in social perception occurred.
source: Our study was also motivated by human psychophysical studies that showed that body and head orientation interact in social perception (Hietanen, 2002; Moors et al., 2015; Vrancken et al., 2017), although it is unclear at which level – sensory or higher – the observed interactions occurred.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous research.

claim: Behavioral studies in humans and monkeys provided evidence for greater body discrimination for upright compared to inverted bodies.
source: Behavioral studies in humans (Griffin and Oswald, 2022) and monkeys (Matsuno and Fujita, 2018) provided evidence for greater body discrimination for upright compared to inverted bodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The body-inversion effect has been interpreted as providing evidence for the holistic encoding of bodies, similar to that proposed for faces.
source: This body-inversion effect has been interpreted as providing evidence for the holistic encoding of bodies, similar to that proposed for faces.
evidence: This is a statement about how previous findings have been interpreted in the literature.

claim: Some studies suggested that the body-inversion effect is driven by the head.
source: Some studies suggested that the body-inversion effect is driven by the head (for review, see Griffin and Oswald, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: Other studies have observed a behavioral body-inversion effect for headless bodies.
source: However, other studies have observed a behavioral body-inversion effect for headless bodies (for a meta-analysis, see Griffin and Oswald, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: No neural correlates of the body-inversion effect for whole bodies have been described at the single-unit level prior to this study.
source: So far, no neural correlates of the body-inversion effect for whole bodies have been described at the single-unit level.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to the current study.

claim: The study recorded responses of units at two posterior–anterior levels of the ventral STS, in and surrounding patches that were activated more by images of monkeys compared to objects in an fMRI study with the same subjects.
source: We recorded the responses of units at two posterior–anterior levels of the ventral STS, in and surrounding patches that were activated more by images of monkeys compared to objects in an fMRI study with the same subjects (Zafirova et al., 2022; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and references a figure showing the recording locations.

claim: Face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT.
source: Because it has been proposed that face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015; Hu et al., 2020; Zafirova et al., 2022), we expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
source: Because it has been proposed that face–body interactions are more prominent in anterior IT (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015; Hu et al., 2020; Zafirova et al., 2022), we expected stronger head–body orientation interactions in the anterior STS (aSTS).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on previous literature.

claim: In experiment 1, 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons were selected for further examination based on their responses to monkeys, faces, or bodies compared to object controls.
source: We took neurons (Materials and methods) for further examination when their mean net response to the monkey, face, or body was at least twice the mean response to the corresponding object control condition. Thus, we obtained 98 aSTS and 100 mSTS neurons, split approximately equally across the two subjects.
evidence: This describes the neuron selection criteria and the resulting sample sizes.

claim: In both aSTS and mSTS regions, the averaged responses of the selected neurons were strongest for the monkey images, followed closely by the body and the face, and much weaker for the objects.
source: In both regions, the averaged responses of the selected neurons were strongest for the monkey images, followed closely by the body and the face, and much weaker for the objects (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the response pattern observed in the data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Some neurons responded stronger to faces than bodies, or vice versa, and showed strong selectivity for different body or face images.
source: Some neurons responded stronger to faces than bodies, or vice versa, and showed strong selectivity for different body or face images (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes variability in neuronal responses observed in the data.

claim: For both subjects and regions, the median MSIs for P1 and P2 were smaller than 0.
source: For both subjects and regions, the median MSIs for P1 and P2 were smaller than 0 (Figure 3A), which agrees with a single-unit study in anterior IT that employed images of real macaques (Zafirova et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes a finding from the data analysis, with reference to a figure and comparison to previous work.

claim: Neurons were observed that responded to either the headless body or head but did not respond to the whole monkey that included the same body and head.
source: Surprisingly, we observed neurons that responded to either the headless body or head but did not respond to the whole monkey that included the same body and head (MSI close to –1; Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes a specific observation from the data.

claim: The weak responses to the monkey were not limited to cases in which the head–body configuration was anatomically impossible.
source: The weak responses to the monkey were not limited to cases in which the head–body configuration was anatomically impossible, that is a straight angle between the head and the body.
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the data regarding anatomically possible vs. impossible configurations.

claim: Cases in which MSI was between –0.9 and –1 included 53% and 41% of natural head–body configurations in aSTS and mSTS, respectively.
source: In fact, cases in which MSI was between –0.9 and –1 included 53% and 41% of natural head–body configurations in aSTS and mSTS, respectively.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative data about the proportion of natural configurations with very negative MSI values.

claim: Only a minority of neurons demonstrated strong superadditive responses to the monkey (MSI between 0.9 and 1: 4.3% and 6.2% in aSTS and mSTS, respectively).
source: In line with a previous study (Zafirova et al., 2024), only a minority of neurons demonstrated strong superadditive responses to the monkey (MSI between 0.9 and 1: 4.3% and 6.2% in aSTS and mSTS, respectively).
evidence: This provides specific quantitative data about the proportion of neurons with superadditive responses, with comparison to previous work.

claim: Heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
source: These data show that heads and bodies interact at the level of the STS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MSI analysis data.

claim: The large majority of neurons showed a significant main effect (p < 0.05) of body orientation followed by a main effect of head orientation.
source: The large majority of neurons showed a significant main effect (p < 0.05) of body orientation followed by a main effect of head orientation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes the results of two-way ANOVA analyses on neuronal responses.

claim: A large fraction of neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation for both centerings (MC and HC) and poses (P1 and P2) in each region (aSTS and mSTS).
source: Importantly, a large fraction of neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation. This was true for both centerings (MC and HC) and poses (P1 and P2) in each region (aSTS and mSTS, Figure 3B).
evidence: This describes a key finding from the two-way ANOVA analyses.

claim: The median correlations of responses to the 64 head–body configurations between MC and HC were 0.68 and 0.57 in aSTS and mSTS, respectively, indicating position tolerance of the orientation selectivity in both regions.
source: The median correlations were 0.68 and 0.57 in aSTS and mSTS, respectively (Figure 3C), indicating position tolerance of the orientation selectivity in both regions.
evidence: This describes quantitative results from correlation analyses assessing position tolerance.

claim: aSTS showed significantly higher correlations than mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.008).
source: In line with its higher hierarchical stage and thus expected higher location tolerance, aSTS showed significantly higher correlations than mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p = 0.008; tested after averaging the correlation coefficients of the poses per neuron; n = 75 aSTS and n = 77 mSTS neurons).
evidence: This describes a statistical comparison between the two regions.

claim: The higher correlations for aSTS were not a result of differences in response reliability between the two regions.
source: The higher correlations for aSTS were not a result of differences in response reliability between the two regions: the median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation (Materials and methods) was 0.82 and 0.81 for the MC and HC aSTS neurons (n = 131 cases) and 0.85 and 0.89 for the MC and HC mSTS neurons (n = 126 cases).
evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation for the regional difference.

claim: The relatively higher reliability for mSTS shows that the lower correlation of the head–body orientation selectivity between the two centerings for mSTS neurons is not due to lower reliability.
source: The relatively higher reliability for mSTS shows that the lower correlation of the head–body orientation selectivity between the two centerings for mSTS neurons is not due to lower reliability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reliability data.

claim: Correcting the correlations for reliability showed a lower median corrected correlation for mSTS (median: 0.72) compared to aSTS (0.90).
source: Furthermore, correcting the correlations for reliability showed a lower median corrected correlation for mSTS (median: 0.72) compared to aSTS (0.90).
evidence: This describes the results of reliability-corrected correlation analyses.

claim: In aSTS, 24% of the neurons responding for both centerings of a pose (n = 135) showed a significant interaction in both centerings, and this proportion was similar for mSTS (26%; n = 127).
source: In aSTS, 24% of the neurons responding for both centerings of a pose (n = 135) showed a significant interaction in both centerings, and this proportion was similar for mSTS (26%; n = 127; Figure 3B).
evidence: This provides quantitative data on the proportion of neurons showing position-tolerant interactions.

claim: For neuron and pose combinations with significant head–body interactions in both centerings, the correlations between responses to the 64 head–body orientation conditions were similar to those observed in the whole population.
source: Notably, for neuron and pose combinations with significant head–body interactions in both centerings, the correlations between responses to the 64 head–body orientation conditions were similar to those observed in the whole population (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes a comparison of correlation values for a subset of neurons.

claim: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS.
source: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS, whereas it was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
evidence: This describes quantitative results from residual correlation analyses.

claim: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
source: The median correlation between the residuals of the two centerings was 0.23 (quartiles: 0.08–0.36; n = 33) for mSTS, whereas it was 0.41 (0.21–0.55; n = 33; median larger than 0: p = 9.35e−07) for aSTS, which was significantly greater than for mSTS (Wilcoxon rank-sum test; p = 0.008).
evidence: This describes quantitative results from residual correlation analyses with statistical testing.

claim: The data demonstrate a position tolerance of the interaction of head and body orientation in aSTS, but less so in mSTS.
source: These data demonstrate a position tolerance of the interaction of head and body orientation in aSTS, but less so in mSTS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the residual correlation analyses.

claim: Some neurons were tuned to a particular combination of a head and body orientation irrespective of centering.
source: Interestingly, some neurons (e.g. Figure 3D) were tuned to a particular combination of a head and body orientation irrespective of centering (e.g. the third aSTS example neuron of Figure 3D).
evidence: This describes an observation from example neurons shown in a figure.

claim: The tuning for head–body orientation generalized across the two poses for the population of mSTS and aSTS neurons that responded significantly to each pose.
source: The tuning for head–body orientation generalized across the two poses for the population of mSTS and aSTS neurons that responded significantly to each pose (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a finding from correlation analyses across poses, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: For the zero and straight reference angles, the classification accuracy increased with the absolute difference between the angles, reaching a maximum of about 0.7 classification accuracy for zero versus straight angles.
source: For the zero and straight reference angles, the classification accuracy increased with the absolute difference between the angles, reaching a maximum of about 0.7 classification accuracy for zero versus straight angles.
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the decoding analyses.

claim: Classification accuracies were smaller for mSTS compared to aSTS.
source: Classification accuracies were smaller for mSTS compared to aSTS.
evidence: This describes a comparison of decoding performance between regions.

claim: For the rightward (90°) and leftward (–90°) right angles as references, classification scores were low, which contrasts with the higher scores for the same 180° orientation difference when the angles were zero and straight.
source: Surprisingly, for the rightward (90°) and leftward (–90°) right angles as references, classification scores were low (Figure 4B), which contrasts with the higher scores for the same 180° orientation difference when the angles were zero and straight (this difference was significant for both centerings and poses in aSTS; all p-values <0.01).
evidence: This describes a surprising pattern in the decoding results with statistical testing.

claim: Classification scores tended to be higher for 90° differences in angles (e.g. right vs. straight) than for the 180° difference (rightward vs. leftward right angles) for the rightward or leftward right reference angles.
source: Classification scores tended to be higher for 90° differences in angles (e.g. right vs. straight) than for the 180° difference (rightward vs. leftward right angles) for the rightward or leftward right reference angles.
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the decoding analyses.

claim: The decoding accuracies showed the same pattern, although were higher, when training and testing were performed with the same centering, requiring no generalization across locations.
source: The decoding accuracies showed the same pattern, although were higher, when training and testing were performed with the same centering, requiring no generalization across locations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes results from additional decoding analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: A neuron-dropping analysis applied to the decoding of zero versus straight angles for the aSTS sample suggested that less than half of the neurons contributed positively to the decoding.
source: A neuron-dropping analysis applied to the decoding of zero versus straight angles for the aSTS sample (MC training and HC testing) suggested that less than half of the neurons contributed positively to the decoding (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes results from a neuron-dropping analysis shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Most but not all of the 10 'best' neurons showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation.
source: Most but not all of the 10 'best' neurons, that is those that contributed most to the decoding, showed a significant interaction between head and body orientation.
evidence: This describes a finding from the neuron-dropping analysis regarding the properties of the most informative neurons.

claim: More of the 10 'best' neurons (at least 50% (95% confidence interval: 19–81%)) showed individually a significant effect of head–body orientation angle on their responses than expected for a random sample of the population of neurons (maximal expected percentage 16%).
source: Furthermore, more of the 10 'best' neurons (at least 50% (95% confidence interval: 19–81%)) showed individually a significant effect of head–body orientation angle on their responses (one-way ANOVA; p < 0.05) than expected for a random sample of the population of neurons (maximal expected percentage 16%; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2 for more details).
evidence: This describes a statistical comparison of the properties of the best neurons versus the population.

claim: The tuning profiles of the 'best' neurons were diverse, suggesting population coding of head–body orientation angle.
source: Nonetheless, the tuning profiles were diverse (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting population coding of head–body orientation angle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diversity of tuning profiles observed in the data.

claim: For P1, the performance accuracies for the aSTS sample were well above chance for the zero versus straight angle decoding when training and testing on different orientations.
source: For P1, the performance accuracies for the aSTS sample were well above chance for the zero versus straight angle decoding, and, as before, were lower for the leftward versus rightward right angle decoding (Figure 5B; for brevity, we will refer to these angles as left and right angles, respectively, below).
evidence: This describes results from a more stringent decoding analysis with generalization across orientations.

claim: For P2, the performance accuracies for zero versus straight angles were barely above chance and were at a similar level as those for the right versus left angle decoding for two of the four centering and orientation training–test combinations.
source: However, for the other two combinations, the performance accuracies for the zero versus straight angles were barely above chance and were at a similar level as those for the right versus left angle decoding (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes results from the decoding analysis for P2 showing different patterns for different training-test combinations.

claim: The interaction between generalization across orientation and centering for P2 is likely related to the larger variations in the eccentricity of the head when changing the orientation and centering of the standing avatar.
source: This interaction between generalization across orientation and centering for P2 is likely related to the larger variations in the eccentricity of the head when changing the orientation and centering of the standing avatar (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference about the cause of the observed pattern, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: When generalization across orientation but not across centering was required, accuracies for P1 and P2 were similar for all decodings.
source: Nonetheless, when generalization across orientation but not across centering was required, accuracies for P1 and P2 were similar for all decodings (for the zero vs. straight angle: classification accuracies for P1 ranging from 0.64 to 0.72 and for P2 ranging from 0.66 to 0.72; for the right vs. left angle decoding: P1 0.49–0.54 and P2 0.48–0.56).
evidence: This describes results from decoding analyses without generalization across centering.

claim: The marked difference in accuracy between the zero versus straight angle decoding and the right versus left angle decoding in aSTS was not trivially due to differences in mean response strength since there was no consistent effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength across poses.
source: The marked difference in accuracy between the zero versus straight angle decoding and the right versus left angle decoding in aSTS was not trivially due to differences in mean response strength since there was no consistent effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength across poses (Friedman ANOVA; all p-values for both poses and centerings >0.1).
evidence: This describes a control analysis ruling out an alternative explanation for the decoding results.

claim: The confusion between left and right angle configurations suggests that this neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
source: The left and right angles have the same absolute angle between head and body (90°), only the sign of the angle differs with respect to the anatomical midline (90° vs. –90°). The confusion between these configurations suggests that this neuronal population is relatively insensitive to the sign of the angle.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decoding results.

claim: Close-to-chance decoding was observed for 45° versus –45° angles and 135° versus –135° angles.
source: We observed a close-to-chance decoding of 45° versus –45° angles and 135° versus –135° angles, unlike the better classification accuracy for the same 90° differences between angles of 0° and 90° or 180° and –90°, the latter but not the former differing in the absolute angle between head and body.
evidence: This describes additional decoding results supporting the insensitivity to sign.

claim: Configurations that differ in absolute angle (45° versus –135° and 135° versus –45°) produced good decoding performance, better than the left versus right angles, which differed only in sign.
source: Other configurations that differ in absolute angle also produced good decoding performance: 45° versus –135° and 135° versus –45°, better than the left versus right angles, which differed only in sign (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes additional decoding results supporting the importance of absolute angle differences.

claim: Neurons in anterior IT are less sensitive to differences between mirror-symmetric images.
source: Neurons in anterior IT are less sensitive to differences between mirror-symmetric images (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Rollenhagen and Olson, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for the lateral head and body orientations for P2 and face orientations of P1.
source: The distance matrices showed evidence for mirror-symmetric responses for the lateral head and body orientations for P2 and face orientations of P1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes results from distance matrix analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Mirror symmetry was less the case for the body of P1, which fits the poorer image symmetry of the body in the case of the P1 lateral views.
source: Mirror symmetry was less the case for the body of P1, which fits the poorer image symmetry of the body in the case of the P1 lateral views.
evidence: This is an inference relating the neural data to properties of the stimuli.

claim: The lower sensitivity for mirror-symmetric heads or bodies may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body angles that differed only in their sign.
source: Thus, the lower sensitivity for mirror-symmetric heads or bodies may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body angles that differed only in their sign.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism underlying the observed decoding pattern.

claim: The difference in decoding accuracy between the zero versus straight angle and the left versus right angle cannot be fully attributed to the mirror symmetry of the avatar images.
source: However, the difference in decoding accuracy between the zero versus straight angle and the left versus right angle, especially when training on the 'x' orientations and testing on '+' orientations (Figure 5), cannot be fully attributed to the mirror symmetry of the avatar images.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analyses that rules out mirror symmetry as the sole explanation.

claim: Spike sorting yielded 497 aSTS (M1 = 280; M2 = 217) and 1856 mSTS (M1 = 804; M2 = 1052) units that responded selectively to the 16 monkey conditions in experiment 2.
source: Spike sorting yielded 497 aSTS (M1 = 280; M2 = 217) and 1856 mSTS (M1 = 804; M2 = 1052) units that responded selectively to the 16 monkey conditions (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the sample sizes obtained in experiment 2.

claim: A highly similar pattern of decoding was found in experiment 2 compared to that obtained with the smaller sample of single units of experiment 1.
source: We found a highly similar pattern (n = 430 units; equated across the two regions and subjects; randomly sampled per subject per resampling; Figure 6B) compared to that obtained with the smaller sample of single units of experiment 1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a replication of the main decoding findings in a larger sample.

claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracy for the zero versus straight angles was about 0.9.
source: For aSTS, the classification accuracy for the zero versus straight angles was about 0.9 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This describes a specific decoding result from experiment 2.

claim: In experiment 2, classification accuracy for the right versus left angles was much lower than that obtained for zero versus right angle, or straight versus left angle, differing in absolute angle (p < 0.01).
source: Again, classification accuracy for the right versus left angles, differing only in their sign, was much lower than that obtained for zero versus right angle, or straight versus left angle, differing in absolute angle (Figure 6B; p < 0.01).
evidence: This describes a replication of the key decoding pattern in experiment 2 with statistical testing.

claim: The classification accuracy for mSTS units in experiment 2 was again lower than for aSTS, although no generalization across centering conditions was required for this decoding.
source: The classification accuracy for mSTS units was again lower than for aSTS (Figure 6B), although no generalization across centering conditions was required for this decoding.
evidence: This describes a regional difference in decoding performance in experiment 2.

claim: In mSTS in experiment 2, there was no difference in decoding accuracy for the zero versus straight angle and right versus left angle.
source: Importantly, in mSTS there was no difference in decoding accuracy for the zero versus straight angle and right versus left angle.
evidence: This describes a key difference between aSTS and mSTS in the decoding pattern.

claim: The reliability of the responses of the units was similar for aSTS (median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation; M1: 0.70; M2: 0.69) and mSTS (median corrected r: M1: 0.72; M2: 0.71) in experiment 2.
source: The reliability of the responses of the units was similar for aSTS (median Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlation; M1: 0.70; M2: 0.69) and mSTS (median corrected r: M1: 0.72; M2: 0.71) and therefore cannot explain the difference in classification accuracy between the two regions.
evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation for regional differences.

claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images.
source: For aSTS, the classification accuracies for the sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), and no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the sums (all p's > 0.4).
evidence: This describes results from decoding analyses using summed responses to isolated heads and bodies.

claim: For aSTS in experiment 2, no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the head–body sums (all p's > 0.4).
source: For aSTS, the classification accuracies for the sums were markedly lower than those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), and no difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles was present for the sums (all p's > 0.4).
evidence: This describes a key finding from the sum decoding analysis.

claim: The lower classification accuracy for the head–body sums in aSTS is not due to a lower reliability of the summed responses compared to the whole-body responses.
source: The lower classification accuracy for the head–body sums is not due to a lower reliability of the summed responses compared to the whole-body responses (Spearman–Brown corrected split-half Pearson correlations; median whole-body r: M1: 0.7; M2: 0.69; sums r: M1: 0.76; M2: 0.66).
evidence: This describes reliability analyses that rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: The difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles requires the simultaneous presence of the head and body.
source: These data suggest that the difference in classification accuracy between the zero versus straight angles and left versus right angles requires the simultaneous presence of the head and body.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of decoding for whole monkeys versus summed head and body responses.

claim: For mSTS in experiment 2, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images.
source: For mSTS, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), suggesting no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
evidence: This describes results from the sum decoding analysis for mSTS.

claim: The similar classification accuracies for head–body sums and monkey images in mSTS suggest no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
source: For mSTS, the classification accuracies for the head–body sums were similar to those obtained for the monkey images (Figure 6B), suggesting no genuine encoding of the head–body angle in this region.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mSTS sum decoding results.

claim: Head- and body-selective aSTS units showed, as a population, a similar decoding bias for zero versus straight angles and both confused the left and right angles.
source: Head- and body-selective aSTS units showed, as a population, a similar decoding bias for zero versus straight angles and both confused the left and right angles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes results from analyses subdividing units by head/body selectivity.

claim: A higher mean response was observed for the upright compared to the inverted preferred orientation of the whole monkey for each pose, in each region of each subject in experiment 3.
source: We observed for each pose, in each region of each subject, a higher mean response for the upright compared to the inverted preferred orientation of the whole monkey (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on data pooled across monkeys: p's in Figure 7C; population PSTHs (Peri-Stimulus Time Histograms) in Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a key finding from experiment 3 regarding the body-inversion effect on response strength.

claim: Upright heads showed across subjects consistently and significantly greater responses than to inverted heads only for P2 in mSTS but not for the other pose or region.
source: Selecting units that responded either to the upright or inverted heads showed less consistent inversion effects for the head than observed for the monkey: upright heads showed across subjects consistently and significantly greater responses than to inverted heads only for P2 in mSTS but not for the other pose or region (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes results from analyses of responses to isolated heads in experiment 3.

claim: The inversion effect for headless bodies was less consistent than for the whole monkey in experiment 3.
source: The same held for the headless body for those units that responded to either the upright or inverted bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes results from analyses of responses to isolated bodies in experiment 3.

claim: The inversion effect was consistently present for the head–body configurations, and less so for the face and body only.
source: Thus, the inversion effect was consistently present for the head–body configurations, and less so for the face and body only.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the inversion effect analyses in experiment 3.

claim: The mean decoding accuracy was significantly higher (all p-values <0.01) for upright compared to inverted monkeys for both poses in aSTS (P1: upright versus inverted: 0.89 vs. 0.82; P2: 0.89 vs. 0.71, with standard deviations SD = 0.02) and mSTS (P1: 0.89 vs. 0.79; P2: 0.93 vs. 0.75; SDs ranging between 0.01 and 0.02).
source: The mean decoding accuracy was significantly higher (all p-values <0.01; Materials and methods) for upright compared to inverted monkeys for both poses in aSTS (P1: upright versus inverted: 0.89 vs. 0.82; P2: 0.89 vs. 0.71, with standard deviations SD = 0.02) and mSTS (P1: 0.89 vs. 0.79; P2: 0.93 vs. 0.75; SDs ranging between 0.01 and 0.02).
evidence: This describes results from decoding analyses of whole-body orientation for upright versus inverted images.

claim: For both poses in experiment 3, the upright images showed again a higher classification performance for the zero versus straight angles and the lowest for the left versus right angles.
source: For both poses (n = 460 responsive aSTS units; an equal number of units randomly sampled per subject per resampling), the upright images showed again a higher classification performance for the zero versus straight angles and the lowest for the left versus right angles (Figure 7B).
evidence: This describes a replication of the key decoding pattern for upright images in experiment 3.

claim: The classification accuracy for head–body angle decoding dropped significantly (zero versus straight angle; all p-values <0.01) for the inverted bodies.
source: The classification accuracy dropped significantly (zero versus straight angle; all p-values <0.01; n = 100 resamplings; Materials and methods) for the inverted bodies (Figure 7B), and this drop in classification accuracy tended to be larger for the zero versus straight angle decoding than for the left versus right angle decoding (the difference between upright and inverted left versus right angle decoding not significant for the two poses; p = 0.2 and 0.18).
evidence: This describes a key finding from experiment 3 regarding the effect of inversion on head–body angle decoding.

claim: The drop in classification accuracy for inverted bodies tended to be larger for the zero versus straight angle decoding than for the left versus right angle decoding.
source: The classification accuracy dropped significantly (zero versus straight angle; all p-values <0.01; n = 100 resamplings; Materials and methods) for the inverted bodies (Figure 7B), and this drop in classification accuracy tended to be larger for the zero versus straight angle decoding than for the left versus right angle decoding (the difference between upright and inverted left versus right angle decoding not significant for the two poses; p = 0.2 and 0.18).
evidence: This describes a pattern in the inversion effect on decoding.

claim: The decoding of the head–body orientation angle is impaired when inverting the monkey image.
source: Thus, the decoding of the head–body orientation angle is impaired when inverting the monkey image.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inversion decoding results.

claim: The stronger inversion effect for the zero versus straight angles decoding suggests that the head–body angle signal in aSTS depends on the global head–body configuration and is not driven merely by inversion-invariant local features.
source: The stronger inversion effect for the zero versus straight angles decoding suggests that the head–body angle signal in aSTS depends on the global head–body configuration and is not driven merely by inversion-invariant local features.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of inversion effects on decoding.

claim: The marked generalization across head–body configuration orientation observed in experiment 1 for P1 would not be expected if local features of individual images were employed by the classifier.
source: This aligns with the marked generalization across head–body configuration orientation that we observed in experiment 1 for P1 (training using four orientations and testing using the other four); such across-orientation generalization would not be expected if local features of individual images were employed by the classifier.
evidence: This is an inference relating the inversion results to the generalization results from experiment 1.

claim: The head–body angle signal is less reliable for inverted head–body configurations, showing a strong inversion effect.
source: This signal is less reliable for inverted head–body configurations, showing a strong inversion effect.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study summarized in the Discussion.

claim: The study could decode the orientation of the head–body configurations, which is an ecologically important property.
source: We could decode the orientation of the head–body configurations, which is an ecologically important property.
evidence: This is a statement about one of the study's findings and its ecological relevance.

claim: From the same population of neurons, the study could also decode the angle between the head and the body, irrespective of the orientation of the configuration.
source: From the same population of neurons, we could also decode the angle between the head and the body, irrespective of the orientation of the configuration (Figure 4A).
evidence: This describes a key finding about orientation-invariant decoding of head–body angle.

claim: Decoding of head–body configuration in the aSTS confused to a greater extent configurations in which the head and body orientation angles differ only in their sign.
source: Remarkably, decoding of head–body configuration in the aSTS confused to a greater extent configurations in which the head and body orientation angles differ only in their sign (e.g. head turned to the left vs. to the right with respect to the body).
evidence: This is a main finding discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The confusion of configurations differing only in sign is quite a robust effect in the aSTS, observed in three different experiments.
source: The latter is quite a robust effect in the aSTS: we observed it in three different experiments.
evidence: This emphasizes the robustness of the finding across experiments.

claim: Images that differ only in the sign of the head–body angle are also to some extent mirror-symmetric.
source: Images, especially of the standing pose, that differ only in the sign of the head–body angle are also to some extent mirror-symmetric.
evidence: This is an observation about the stimulus properties.

claim: The population of single aSTS neurons showed evidence of a lower sensitivity of mirror-symmetrical views for heads and bodies.
source: Our population of single aSTS neurons showed evidence of a lower sensitivity of mirror-symmetrical views for heads and bodies.
evidence: This describes a finding from the distance matrix analyses.

claim: One factor that may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body orientation angles that differ only in sign is mirror symmetry.
source: Thus, one factor that may have contributed to the lower decoding of head–body orientation angles that differ only in sign is mirror symmetry.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: The highest decoding of the head–body angle occurred for the zero versus straight angles, which is a classification of a frequently observed head–body configuration versus an anatomically impossible angle.
source: The highest decoding of the head–body angle occurred for the zero versus straight angles. Basically, this is a classification of a frequently observed head–body configuration, that is the same orientation of head and body, versus an anatomically impossible angle, at least for primates.
evidence: This describes the best-decoded angle pair and relates it to anatomical possibility.

claim: All well-decodable absolute differences in angles consisted of a possible versus an impossible angle, while angles that differ only in their sign are either both anatomically possible or both impossible.
source: In fact, all well-decodable absolute differences in angles consisted of a possible versus an impossible angle, while angles that differ only in their sign are either both anatomically possible or both impossible.
evidence: This is an observation about the pattern of decodable angle pairs.

claim: The anatomical possibility factor may explain the better decoding for configurations that differ in their absolute angle.
source: Thus, this anatomical possibility factor may explain the better decoding for configurations that differ in their absolute angle.
evidence: This is a speculation about a potential explanation for the decoding pattern.

claim: Dissociating the anatomical possibility factor from absolute versus signed angle difference, or mirror symmetry, is not trivial, since these three factors covary in monkey configurations when manipulating the orientation of the head and body.
source: However, dissociating this factor from absolute versus signed angle difference, or mirror symmetry, is not trivial, since these three factors covary in monkey configurations when manipulating the orientation of the head and body.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study design.

claim: The decoding of whole-monkey orientation was present in mSTS and aSTS, which aligns with previous studies.
source: The decoding of whole-monkey orientation, which can be based on head and/or body orientation, was present in mSTS and aSTS, which aligns with previous studies (Bao et al., 2020; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Kumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes a finding that is consistent with previous literature.

claim: In line with previous studies, the decoding of head and body orientation was better in mSTS compared to aSTS.
source: In line with previous studies (Kumar et al., 2019; Meyers et al., 2015), the decoding of head and body orientation was better in mSTS compared to aSTS (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes a finding consistent with previous literature, with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The decoding of head–body configuration showed the opposite trend to head/body orientation decoding: it was worse in mSTS than in aSTS.
source: However, the decoding of head–body configuration, that is head–body orientation angle, showed the opposite trend: it was worse in mSTS than in aSTS.
evidence: This describes a key finding showing a regional difference in head–body angle decoding.

claim: The regional difference in head–body configuration decoding agrees with previous work that suggested the presence of head–body integration in the anterior but less so in the posterior temporal cortex.
source: This agrees with previous work that suggested the presence of head–body integration in the anterior but less so in the posterior temporal cortex (Fisher and Freiwald, 2015; Hu et al., 2020; Zafirova et al., 2022).
evidence: This relates the current findings to previous literature.

claim: No significant effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength was observed, indicating that anatomically possible and impossible configurations elicited statistically similar averaged responses.
source: We observed no significant effect of head–body orientation angle on mean response strength, indicating that anatomically possible and impossible configurations elicited statistically similar averaged responses.
evidence: This describes a finding about response strength across different head–body angles.

claim: A previous study in which responses to head–body configurations in which the body and head were misaligned were lower than those for a natural head–body configuration targeted a patch that only partially overlapped the fMRI-defined monkey patch of the present study.
source: This differs from a previous study in which responses to head–body configurations in which the body and head were misaligned were lower than those for a natural head–body configuration (Zafirova et al., 2024). However, that study targeted a patch that was defined in fMRI by contrasting aligned versus misaligned head–body configurations, which only partially overlapped the fMRI-defined monkey patch of the present study.
evidence: This compares the current findings to a previous study and notes differences in recording locations.

claim: The present study examined head–body orientation interactions, while the previous one examined head–body relative position interactions, which are fundamentally different.
source: Furthermore, the present study examined head–body orientation interactions, while the previous one head–body relative position interactions, which are fundamentally different.
evidence: This notes a key difference between the current and a previous study.

claim: The present study suggests that mSTS and aSTS neurons respond equally strongly to anatomically possible and impossible head–body configurations, at least when these are defined by the head–body orientation angle.
source: Nonetheless, the present study suggests that mSTS and aSTS neurons respond equally strongly to anatomically possible and impossible head–body configurations, at least when these are defined by the head–body orientation angle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the response strength analyses.

claim: As a population, mSTS and aSTS neurons can distinguish strikingly well the possible and impossible configurations since these differ in their absolute angle.
source: However, as a population, they can distinguish strikingly well the possible and impossible configurations since these differ in their absolute angle (see above).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analyses.

claim: Based on the electrophysiological data, one would predict that, at the behavioral level, the discrimination of head–body orientation angle, irrespective of the viewpoint of the avatar, would be more accurate for zero versus straight angles compared to right versus left angles.
source: Based on our electrophysiological data, one would predict that, at the behavioral level, the discrimination of head–body orientation angle, irrespective of the viewpoint of the avatar, would be more accurate for zero versus straight angles compared to right versus left angles, but this remains to be tested psychophysically.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the neural data that requires future behavioral testing.

claim: The work demonstrates for the first time an inversion effect for bodies with heads in the ventral bank of the STS.
source: Our work demonstrates for the first time an inversion effect for bodies with heads in the ventral bank of the STS.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the inversion effect findings.

claim: Previous studies reported a higher response to upright compared to inverted bodies in the STS, but the neurons in these studies were searched with upright bodies.
source: Previous studies reported a higher response to upright compared to inverted bodies in the STS (Ashbridge et al., 2000; Popivanov et al., 2015), but the neurons in these studies were searched with upright bodies.
evidence: This compares the current study to previous studies and notes a methodological difference.

claim: In the current study, a search bias cannot explain the body-inversion effect since responsive units were selected using both upright and inverted images.
source: However, in our study, a search bias cannot explain the body-inversion effect since we selected responsive units using both upright and inverted images.
evidence: This explains why the current study's findings are not confounded by search bias.

claim: A body-inversion effect has been observed in both humans and monkeys at the behavioral level.
source: A body-inversion effect has been observed in both humans and monkeys at the behavioral level (Griffin and Oswald, 2022; Matsuno and Fujita, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Some but not all human studies observed a stronger inversion effect for a body with than without a head.
source: Some but not all human studies (see Griffin and Oswald, 2022 for a meta-analysis) observed a stronger inversion effect for a body with than without a head.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a meta-analysis.

claim: The current data suggest a more consistent inversion effect for head–body configurations compared to headless bodies and heads in STS.
source: Our data suggest also a more consistent inversion effect for head–body configurations compared to headless bodies and heads in STS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inversion effect analyses in experiment 3.

claim: The body-inversion effect likely results from greater exposure to upright than inverted bodies during development, although this remains to be proved.
source: The body-inversion effect likely results from greater exposure to upright than inverted bodies during development, although, as for the face-inversion effect, this remains to be proved (Kobylkov and Vallortigara, 2024).
evidence: This is a speculation about the developmental origin of the inversion effect, with a citation noting it remains unproven.

claim: The monkeys were not exposed to the anatomically impossible head–body orientations, but still, the responses to these configurations were similar to those to anatomically possible configurations.
source: Our monkeys were not exposed to the anatomically impossible head–body orientations, but still, the responses to these configurations were similar to those to anatomically possible configurations.
evidence: This is an observation about the monkeys' experience and the neural responses.

claim: The apparent discrepancy between the head-inversion effect and the anatomically (im)possible head–body orientation configuration may result from both head and body being in an infrequent orientation in the case of inversion while for the impossible head–body orientation configuration either the head or the body, but not both, might be at an infrequently exposed orientation.
source: This apparent discrepancy between the head-inversion effect and the anatomically (im)possible head–body orientation configuration may result from both head and body being in an infrequent orientation in the case of inversion while for the impossible head–body orientation configuration either the head or the body, but not both, might be at an infrequently exposed orientation.
evidence: This is a speculation about why inversion has a stronger effect than anatomical impossibility.

claim: The experiments were performed with two male rhesus monkeys (M1 and M2; Macaca mulatta, 6–7 years, 11–12 kg).
source: The experiments were performed with the two male rhesus monkeys (M1 and M2; Macaca mulatta, 6–7 years, 11–12 kg; Supplier: BPRC, Rijswijk, The Netherlands) which took part in our fMRI study (Zafirova et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: All experimental procedures and animal care complied with national and European regulations and were approved by the Animal Ethical Committee at KU Leuven (reference number: 105/2019).
source: All experimental procedures and animal care complied with national and European regulations and were approved by the Animal Ethical Committee at KU Leuven (reference number: 105/2019).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.
